https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxe.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Lake Kariba, which sits on Zimbabwe's border with Zambia, is one of the world's largest man-made reservoirs By Basillioh Rukanga Published 55 minutes ago Multiple people are feared dead after a boat carrying 95 people sank on Kariba dam in Zimbabwe, with rescue operations under way. Police said 90 passengers and five crew were onboard the vessel when it capsized on Tuesday, but it may have been overloaded, with other reports pointing to a higher number based on the registered ticket sales. The vessel, which had left in the morning in bad weather according to a witness who spoke to AFP, may have been hit by a wave and overturned. Lake Kariba, which straddles the border with Zambia, is one of the world's largest man-made reservoirs, supporting transport and fishing and providing vital hydroelectric power to both countries. The AP news agency quoted Zimbabwe's Civil Protection Unit as saying that registered ticket sales showed 114 adults were on board the vessel. There could also have been an unknown number of children below ticketing age, it added. Mutsa Murombedzi, a local member of parliament, posted a video on X , external of what she said was the boat at the start of the journey, adding that locals had been using it to travel across the lake to Kariba town, a journey that takes about five hours. "We have very hard questions that require honest answers. The officials must release the correct number of people who were onboard," she wrote. Police said more details, including the number of people who have died and those rescued, will be "released in due course". https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy4z.text: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about the fatal Philippines ferry fire By Virma Simonette Rivera ,Â Reporting from Manila Â and Â Kelly Ng Published 10 September 2026, 05:08 BST Updated 3 hours ago At least five people have died and 86 are missing after a fire broke out on a ferry in the Philippines, the country's coastguard said. The MV June Aster, which set off from Manila ferrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron when it caught fire. The blaze, which erupted at 18:45 local time (10:45 GMT) Wednesday, was still burning as of 11:00 on Thursday. The strong currents and thick smoke were a challenge to those working to extinguish it, the coastguard said. A survivor said he floated in the sea for two hours before he got rescued. "It was cold. If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died," Roland Lerma told the BBC. Image source, Philippine Coast Guard Image caption, The fire broke out as the vessel was reaching the tourist hotspot of Coron in Palawan Video clips shared by the coastguard on Wednesday night showed the vessel engulfed in flames and people being pulled out of the water into rescue boats. The cause of the fire remains under investigation, the coastguard said. The coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest the fire started in the cargo hold, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, the coastguard said. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted. Forty-three people have been rescued but it is unclear how many have sustained injuries. Seven of the survivors were taken to a hospital in Culion, a larger neighbouring island, which has higher bed capacity and more comprehensive healthcare services. A first responder told the BBC they had never seen such a disaster in Coron, calling it "really heartbreaking". "I was one of the people who carried and transported the casualties to the hospital last night," they said, adding that the ferry was an hour away from its destination. The survivors were taken to an evacuation centre in Barangay Turda, which sits just north of Marcilla. The state of their injuries is unclear. 'People were trampling me': Philippine ferry fire survivor recalls narrow escape Published 52 minutes ago Image source, Reuters Image caption, Footage from the coastguard show the vessel engulfed in flames Rai Garcia has three family friends among those missing. Mae Lorraine Galera-Navoa, who is the sister of Garcia's brother-in-law, had travelled to Luzon to attend her father's funeral, accompanied by her husband Elyzer Navoa and their three-year-old daughter Hiraya Joy. They had been travelling home to El Nido in Palawan on board the vessel when it caught fire. "We haven't received any news yet. That's why we had to comment on local news threads just to receive updates," Garcia says. "We still hope and pray for their safety." Garcia and his family made a poster to appeal for information of the family of three using a photo Mae had taken on the ferry and shared with immediate relatives. Others have posted on the Philippine Coast Guard's Facebook page asking for information of their missing loved ones. "Please can you find my sibling," read one comment. Maritime accidents are common in the Philippines, an archipelago of 7,100 islands. Inter-island ferries are a cheap way to move people and cargo between islands, some of which are inaccessible by air. But there is always the risk of severe weather, monsoon rains and typhoons which can cause turbulent conditions. The country is affected by an average of 20 typhoons every year. Past accidents have also been blamed on poor maintenance and uneven enforcement of safety laws. In 2023, 31 people died after a fire broke out at a passenger ferry in the country's south-western tip. The MV Lady Mary Joy 3 was on its way to Basilan island from Zamboanga city, a major port in the main southern island of Mindanao. But with 86 still missing, this ferry disaster could prove to be among the worst to have happened in the Philippines in recent years. https://www.iowapublicradio.org/arts-lif.text: On Air Now Playing IPR News On Air Now Playing IPR Classical On Air Now Playing IPR Studio One Arts & Life 2 for the Show Movie news, reviews and musings by Nicole Baxter and Clinton Olsasky What we saw at the 2026 Telluride Film Festival: AI debates, Oscar hopefuls and a top-secret screening Iowa Public Radio | By Clinton Olsasky , Nicole Baxter Published September 11, 2026 at 10:28 AM CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Stills courtesy of A24, Bleecker Street, Searchlight Pictures, Netflix, Obscured Pictures and Neon. Over Labor Day weekend every year, the remote, idyllic town of Telluride, Colorado, transforms into a movie lover’s dream. First held in 1974, the Telluride Film Festival has long served as the unofficial kickoff to awards season and has premiered dozens of eventual Oscar nominees and winners throughout its 50-plus-year existence. This year was no exception, with the 53rd year of the festival hosting numerous U.S. and world premieres for films that will no doubt rack up plenty of golden statuettes. Expect to hear a lot more about Wild Horse Nine , La Bola Negra and The Debut over the coming months; all three films were met with rave reviews at Telluride and are sure to have a major presence at the Oscars next year. There were also several illuminating panel discussions with filmmakers, actors and industry experts. The most notable of these was a wide-ranging conversation about AI, featuring both Tristan Harris of the Netflix documentary The Social Dilemma and none other than Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft. Oprah Winfrey was even on hand to moderate a Q&A with mountaineer Jim Morrison, featured in the National Geographic documentary Everest: The Other Side . In addition to Gates and Winfrey, some of the other famous faces spotted at Telluride included Emma Stone, Jesse Eisenberg, Willem Dafoe, Julianne Moore, Barry Jenkins, John Malkovich and Sofia Coppola, just to name a few. 1 of 2 — Telluride Film Festival 2026-5.jpg The 53rd Telluride Film Festival took place Sept. 4-7. in the mountainous, southwest corner of Colorado. The festival takes over the tiny box canyon town, with screening venues sprinkled from end to end. Nicole Baxter / Iowa Public Radio 2 of 2 — Telluride Film Festival 2026-2.jpg Filmmakers, actors, industry leaders and other experts participate in noon seminars in the town park during the festival. On Sept. 6, Julianne Moore (right), Jesse Eisenberg, John Turturro and Kenneth Branagh discussed acting in a conversation moderated by Annette Insdorf (center). Nicole Baxter / Iowa Public Radio The many celebrity sightings and strong slate of awards contenders would have been enough to generate plenty of buzz for this year’s Telluride Film Festival. But all that was overshadowed by a top-secret screening on Sunday night, when several hundred attendees packed into the Werner Herzog Theatre, surrendered their phones to Yondr pouches and were treated to a jaw-dropping, three-hour documentary from the inimitable mind of Nathan Fielder. Below is a recap of our thoughts on that film and six others we saw at the 53rd Telluride Film Festival that are sure to make an impression. Wild Horse Nine John Malkovich attended the Telluride Film Festival as one of this year’s three Silver Medallion recipients, and the recognition was well-deserved. The veteran actor has been turning in award-worthy work on the big screen for decades, but Wild Horse Nine may be the film that finally nabs him his first Oscar. Set in Chile shortly before a CIA-backed coup in 1973, Wild Horse Nine continues director Martin McDonagh’s penchant for pitch-black humor and thorny male relationships. Malkovich is a big part of that, delivering a drolly funny and surprisingly moving lead performance as Chris, an eccentric CIA agent with a terminal illness and a mysterious past. His days numbered, Chris embarks on a trip to Easter Island with his agency partner Lee, played by Sam Rockwell. While there, the two agents become embroiled in a conspiratorial plot that meanders a bit too aimlessly before delivering the goods in a thrilling and satisfying third act. — Clinton Olsasky Tender Loving Care No other filmmaker brings the power of empathy to the screen quite like Mike Leigh, and the legendary British director’s latest (and likely last) film is further proof of that. With Tender Loving Care , Leigh turns his empathetic gaze to two social workers, played by Kate O’Flynn and Alice Bailey Johnson. Their lives unfold alongside an elderly couple at the end of their days, played by Paul Jesson and Marion Bailey, who all but steal the show with a pair of charming, heart-melting performances. Leigh isn’t interested in showcasing just one or two great actors, though. Instead, every performance in Tender Loving Care works together, forming a more richly layered snapshot of not just a single life but of many lives. It’s a beautiful swan song of a film for Leigh, who now appears to be closing out his incomparable career on a fittingly tender note. — C.O. Ink In his latest feature, British director Danny Boyle takes a break from the Rage Virus of his 28 Days Later franchise to focus on another form of infectious outrage: the news. Set in 1969, Ink outlines the origins of media mogul Rupert Murdoch’s early days as a newspaper magnate in London’s printing district. With his trademark kinetic camerawork, Boyle throws viewers into the story during a momentous meeting between Murdoch, played by Guy Pearce, and news editor Larry Lamb, played by Jack O’Connell. Together, the two hatch a plan to revamp an underperforming newspaper into a profitable publication that’s brash, raunchy and loud. Boyle brings his distinct punk-rock style to the story, resulting in a movie that’s as brash, raunchy and loud as its subject matter. This energy propels the narrative for a while, but it ultimately ends up crashing into a messy combination of sex, drugs, murder and some regrettable uses of AI. — Nicole Baxter The Debut The Debut had one of the splashiest, well, debuts at Telluride this year, launching Jesse Eisenberg’s surreal and side-splitting comedy into the upper echelon of Oscar contenders. Featuring a suite of original songs penned by Eisenberg himself, The Debut stars Julianne Moore as Mona, a timid New Jersey housewife who musters up the courage to audition for a musical at her local community theater. Her audition brings her into the orbit of Jerry, a tough but intensely passionate theater director, played by Paul Giamatti. Jerry puts Mona through the ringer as the opening night of the musical nears, pushing her out of her comfort zone and helping her unlock a previously untapped confidence that, at times, devolves into grandiose delusions. The Debut marks a big step forward for Eisenberg as a director, who previously impressed with his Oscar-winning film A Real Pain . Here, he finds a perfect balance between broad comedy and pathos, shining a spotlight on the power of art — and, more importantly, community — to transform us from the inside out. — C.O. Bucking Fastard Werner Herzog was sadly not in attendance at Telluride this year, but his presence was certainly felt with his first narrative feature in seven years. Bucking Fastard is loosely inspired by a news item from the 1980s, a bizarre account of a pair of twin sisters who had a restraining order placed on them by the same man. Herzog takes a number of liberties with this story, transplanting the incident to the current day and casting real-life sisters (but non-twins) Rooney and Kate Mara as the women in question. The Mara sisters are mesmerizing in the dual roles of Jean and Joan, speaking nearly all of their dialogue in unison and bringing both a defiant intensity and childlike naivety to their characters. The film, while never dull, does stray away from a coherent plot at times, but Herzog (mostly) brings it all together in an extended cave sequence that feels like it could have been lifted from one of his breathtaking nature documentaries. — C.O. Fjord One of the most anticipated international films to screen at Telluride was Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord , which months earlier was awarded the top prize at the Cannes Film Festival, securing the Romanian filmmaker the second Palme d’Or of his career. Unlike his previous Palme d’Or winner, 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days , which was set in communist Romania, Mungiu sets Fjord in present-day Scandinavia for an ultra-timely, conversation-sparking family drama. At the center of it all are husband and wife Mihai and Lisbet, played by Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, who are forced to defend their parenting practices — and their religious beliefs — in the wake of abuse accusations. Mungiu has a way of presenting a morally complicated story with a rare degree of neutrality, and Fjord may be his best execution of that kind of storytelling yet. The film has a specific setting and subject matter, but its core message remains universal, warning us of the dangers of political extremism all around us. — N.B. You Can See Everything I was lucky enough to be among the few hundred Telluride attendees to see the world premiere of You Can See Everything , Nathan Fielder’s latest reality-blurring, mind-bending creation. And I’m still not sure what I experienced. The nearly three-hour-long documentary is a roller coaster ride of a movie, opening with Fielder gaining unprecedented access to convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes, roughly one month before her incarceration in 2023. Yes, that means this film has secretly been in the making for the past three years; but in typical Fielder fashion, where it started is far from where it ends up. Beautifully shot, impeccably edited and utterly captivating, You Can See Everything marks the full arrival of Fielder as a major cinematic force. You won’t see anything else like it this year because, well, there hasn’t been anything quite like it ever before. — C.O. He graduated from the University of Northern Iowa, where he earned a bachelor's degree in digital journalism and a minor in film studies. While at UNI, he served as the executive editor and film critic for the Northern Iowan newspaper, as well as co-founder and president of the UNI Film Appreciation Club. https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/a.text: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home World News European Union eyes battle over ‘pervert’ AI glasses SECRET FOOTAGE: A 17-year-old girl told British broadcaster Channel 4 that she had been approached by a man who covertly recorded her and their interaction AFP, BRUSSELS Add TT as Preferred Source Calls are growing louder in Europe for action against “pervert” smart glasses after secretly filmed footage of girls and women appeared online — with a petition in Britain demanding a ban on their sale. Anyone wearing smart glasses can take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an artificial intelligence (AI) assistant, with sales now hitting millions. The devices grabbed attention this summer after a marketing tie-up between Kylie Jenner, beauty mogul and member of the Kardashian dynasty, and tech giant Meta. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wears the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses as he delivers a speech during the Meta Connect in Menlo Park, California, on Sept. 17 last year. Photo: Reuters Since smartphones are now embedded in daily life, “big tech” is increasingly looking to glasses as the next big thing in wearable technology, helped by AI’s advances. A 2013 push by Google failed to take off, but Meta’s smart spectacles, developed in partnership with Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica, have fared much better. Meta sold about 7 million pairs last year, up from a total of 2 million in 2023 and 2024. Others, including Google and Snap, are also preparing to roll out AI-powered glasses. However, with exponential growth came the backlash. Worries reached a peak in the summer in Europe, especially in Britain which saw intense media coverage of so-called “pervert glasses” alongside reports that Meta is developing a facial recognition feature to be integrated into the devices. In one case, a 17-year-old girl told British broadcaster Channel 4 News last month how she had been approached by a man who covertly recorded her and their interaction. Meta said it has taken multiple steps to prevent tampering with the blinking LED light intended to show other people the device is recording — a key concern of critics. “These investments are already having a deterrent effect,” it said, saying that companies offering to disable the LED lights had shut down as a result. In the meantime, Norway’s capital Oslo banned the glasses in schools this week as the government mulls regulating their use and considers a ban on features that enable facial recognition in public. There are similar calls for the EU to take up the issue, while France’s National Commission on Informatics and Liberty data protection watchdog has urged “vigilance.” A Swedish designer, Mateusz Pozar, launched a “Ban Ray” site earlier this year, providing signs to ban smart glasses from venues and selling stickers. Pozar said he started the site after his girlfriend was approached by two men wearing the glasses and recording her, which “freaked her out.” He said he wanted a discussion about how “we as a society feel about this technology” before it becomes ubiquitous. “This is a lever to have a discussion about privacy, personal rights, control over my data,” he said. Pozar also pointed to his concerns about data extraction after reports about Kenya-based workers who reviewed graphic content captured by Meta’s AI glasses. Slovakian Member of the European Parliament Veronika Cifrova Ostrihonova said that she raised the issue with the bloc’s executive after the first cases of women being secretly filmed, seeking to know if the glasses comply with data protection and AI rules. “I am still awaiting an answer,” the Slovak lawmaker said. “We need clear EU rules to protect and strong enforcement to make sure new technologies don’t come at the expense of our fundamental rights,” she said. The European Commission said national data protection authorities were “responsible for monitoring and enforcing” privacy rules. The EU executive would not be drawn on what further action it could take, but the independent European Data Protection Board commissioned a report expected in autumn looking at the glasses’ “social acceptability.” That report would guide the European Parliament, where Member of the European Parliament Alex Agius Saliba said there were concerns across the political spectrum. “We must act as soon as possible,” he said. “For me, they are still pervert glasses,” Saliba said. “As things stand today, we should definitely go for a ban” until they are proven safe, he added. A “Stop Smart Glasses” campaign launched in Britain and Ireland, with a petition and call for supporters to contact stores to stop their sale. The petition has more than 9,100 signatures so far. The British government must respond if it reaches 10,000. One of the campaign’s founders, teacher Guy Holder, said he had several concerns about the glasses including their effects on girls and women and a broader “invasion” of public spaces that could lead to “total surveillance.” “We are also concerned more broadly about an atmosphere in which it feels like anybody can film anybody without their knowledge or consent,” he said. The men work for Kuramoto Ice, a century-old company in Ishikawa on the Sea of Japan coast and one of dozens of Japanese firms producing ultra-clear, premium ice. This luxury product, believed by those in the industry to melt more slowly than regular blocks, is a staple of Japan’s cocktail culture, but its popularity is also spilling over to bars abroad, from the US to Australia, who pay as much as ￥200 (US$1.28) per cube. Kuramoto Ice Buddhist abbot in Thailand arrested over embezzlement 2026-09-12 Thai police yesterday said that they arrested a senior Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling US$2.8 million intended for his monastery, alongside a suspected female accomplice he was having sex with. The case is the latest scandal to hit the clergy in Buddhist-majority Thailand after a sex and extortion case involving senior monks last year prompted public outrage and calls for greater scrutiny of temple finances. Phra Wachirayan Wi, the 66-year-old abbot of the 14th-century Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, was arrested on Thursday on charges including embezzlement and money laundering, lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan said. A 47-year-old woman Mao’s shadow hangs over China 50 years on 2026-09-10 China yesterday marked half a century since the death of Mao Zedong (毛澤東), founder of the People’s Republic, who brought roughly one-quarter of the world’s population under communist rule and whose specter still haunts China’s future. Mao’s death on Sept. 9, 1976, at age 82, mourned by many and welcomed by some who suffered under his nearly three-decade rule, also hastened the end of the Cultural Revolution, a frenzied mass movement he launched in 1966. The party later condemned the Cultural Revolution as a grave error for which Mao bore primary responsibility, but still reveres him, saying his achievements outweigh his mistakes. https://www.dw.com/en/houthi-strike-on-y.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OQAl The Houthis began a new offensive against the internationally-recognized Yemeni government in September [FILE: October 7, 2026] Image: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement At least 50 Yemeni government forces were killed in a strike by Houthi rebels on a military camp in the south of the country on Monday, military officials said. The group fired three ballistic missiles at the al-Alam camp in the province of Shabwa. Some 200 recruits were also wounded, according to the provincial government. The Houthis confirmed that they had targeted the camp. Deadliest attack in recent surge of violence in Yemen Military sources had originally put the death toll at 30, but this rose to at least 50 later in the day, with the Associated Press giving a toll of 53 and citing provincial authorities. "The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa said, according to AFP. Al-Khalifi added that local hospitals had been overwhelmed and some of the more seriously wounded had been transferred to facilities in other provinces. The increased death toll makes Monday's attack one of the deadliest in the recent uptick of violence in Yemen. Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Yemeni government vows response to Houthi attack Fighting in Yemen between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government has been going on for years, but the US-Israeli war on Iran and other factors have sparked renewed fighting in the peninsula, with the Houthis also carrying out major attacks on Saudi Arabian soil . Officials said that the soldiers who were killed and wounded in the attack had been recruits for a new Rapid Intervention force which is supposed to defend the local area. The missiles reportedly struck while they were lining up in formation ahead of training. Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, vowed a "firm response" for the killing of the recruits and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter." Monday's strikes follow several attacks over the weekend that killed more than 30 people in Houthi-held areas. The Houthis have blamed Saudi-led forces for the attacks. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/actualitate/.text: Un bărbat de 40 de ani din oraşul Oţelu Roşu, judeţul Caraş-Severin, şi-a atacat, luni, cu un cuţit soţia şi fiul vitreg, în vârstă de 21 de ani. Tânărul a murit în urma rănilor, iar femeia a fost transportată la spital. Agresorul este în custodia Poliţiei. „În această dimineaţă, ora 04.38, Inspectoratul de Poliţie Judeţean Caraş-Severin a fost sesizat prin apel 112 de o femeie din oraşul Oţelu Roşu că, în urma unui conflict spontan în locuinţă, soţul i-a atacat cu un cuţit pe ea şi pe fiul vitreg de 21 de ani. În urma agresiunii, tânărul de 21 de ani a decedat, iar femeia de 48 de ani a fost preluată de echipajul medical al Serviciului de Ambulanţă şi a fost transportată la spital", a informat, luni, Inspectoratul de Poliţie Judeţean Caraş-Severin, citat de News.ro. Agresorul, în vârstă de 40 de ani, este în custodia Poliţiei, urmând a fi dispuse măsurile legale faţă de acesta. „Până în prezent nu au mai fost alte sesizări în legătură cu persoanele implicate", a precizat Poliţia. Ancheta este desfăşurată de procurorul de caz de la Parchetul de pe lângă Tribunalul Caraş-Severin. Urmărește știrile Digi24.ro și pe Google News

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-exami.text: The European Commission will examine its association agreement with Israel after more than 1.1 million EU citizens signed a petition asking it to do so. "The Commission will meet the organisers [of the petition] to discuss the initiative in detail in the coming weeks. A public hearing will then be organised by the European Parliament," the EU executive said in a press release Thursday. While the examination is unlikely to lead to any substantial changes to the status quo, the number of signatures shows the prominence of the issue of EU-Israel relations among the EU public — and will force the Commission to give an official response. Advertisement Advertisement Out of 136 registered petitions — known as the EU Citizens' Initiative — in more than a decade, only 14 had reached the 1 million-signature threshold required to be officially brought in front of the EU executive. The ECI mechanism requires the Commission to examine petitions signed by more than 1 million EU citizens from more than seven countries. Earlier this year, the Commission rejected a petition to expand abortion financing after it was signed by 1.2 million citizens. The European Left Alliance, an umbrella group for 11 left-wing political parties, started the petition almost two years ago. The group said the EU should suspend its trade and political dialogue with Israel over what it sees as the country's failure to prevent genocide in Gaza. France accounted for the most signatures with 339,479, followed by Italy with 283,863 and Spain with 151,821. The Commission will reply by May 2027 to say whether it plans to take any action in response to the petition. Originally signed in 1995 and coming into force in 2000, the association agreement covers political dialogue and trade between the EU and Israel. The bloc is Israel’s biggest trading partner, accounting for about a third of its total trade in goods with the world in 2025, according to EU data . The wars in Gaza and Lebanon have provoked vehement criticism of Israel and divided European leaders. Advertisement Advertisement
